requirements.requirement: Create the appworker account on node1
requirements.summary: Executor confirmed no pre-existing appworker user, then created it with useradd -m; id output shows uid=1000(appworker) gid=1000(appworker). Account presence was reverified after restart via getent passwd.

requirements.requirement: Limit appworker login sessions to 8,192 open files (nofile) and 256 processes (nproc)
requirements.summary: A limits.d config (/etc/security/limits.d/90-appworker.conf) was written with soft/hard nofile=8192 and soft/hard nproc=256, and enforcement was verified in a real login shell (sudo -u appworker -i) showing ulimit -n=8192 and ulimit -u=256, both before and after the restart.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol on node1 (pre-restart baseline, restart acknowledgement, changed boot identity, recovered account/service/data state)
requirements.summary: Executor captured a pre-restart baseline (boot_id e31962a9…, uptime, passwd entry, limits config), issued a backgrounded 'shutdown -r now' with acknowledgement before disconnect, polled until reconnection (one timeout then success), and captured a post-restart boot_id (0e0335eb…) that differs from the baseline along with a new uptime start time. Post-restart state re-confirms the appworker account and enforced 8192/256 limits. This sequence is corroborated by the fixed global before_prepare and after_executor boot-identity snapshots, which show the identical boot_id transition (e31962a9… → 0e0335eb…), independently cross-checking the executor's restart claim.

overall_summary: The executor satisfied both material outcomes of the task: it created the appworker account on node1 and configured/verified enforced login-session limits of 8,192 open files and 256 processes via limits.d, confirmed live via a real login shell. It additionally completed the mandatory node-restart evidence protocol with a full pre-restart baseline, a restart acknowledgement, a poll-based disconnect/reconnect sequence, a directly observed boot-identity change, and a post-restart re-verification of the account and enforced limits — all independently corroborated by the fixed global lifecycle boot-identity snapshots. Operational hygiene is very good, with only a trivial leftover /tmp/reboot.log file as residue from the restart command.
limitations: The /tmp/reboot.log file left on node1 after the restart was not explicitly assessed by the executor as cleanup-worthy, so its permanence going forward is not directly confirmed beyond the after_executor snapshot.

No dedicated evidence directly shows service-level health checks (e.g., systemd status) immediately after restart beyond the general failed-services and package-health snapshots, though these show no regressions.

operational_hygiene.summary: Reviewing the chronological command trace, every state-changing command has a clear purpose: existence check (read-only), useradd -m (task requirement), writing the limits.d file (task requirement), live ulimit verification (read-only/diagnostic), baseline capture (restart-protocol prerequisite), the restart itself (restart-protocol requirement), polling for reconnection (read-only), and post-restart verification (restart-protocol requirement). No unauthorized or unrelated mutations were found. One minor residue exists: the backgrounded reboot command redirected output to /tmp/reboot.log, which remains present in the after_executor temporary-files snapshot and was not cleaned up. This is a small, low-risk, non-security-relevant leftover file directly produced as a side effect of the required restart action, not an unrelated experiment, so it is scored as a minor deduction rather than a significant hygiene issue. No failed services, no package-health degradation, and no new listening sockets were introduced (socket/PID changes between snapshots reflect normal service restarts across the reboot, not new exposure).
